etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in a gloss of the Nihon Shoki (720) and Man'yōshū (759) in the ideographic spelling 笠. In turn, from reconstructed Proto-Japonic *kasa (“rain hat”). Possibly related to 重なる (kasanaru, “to overlap, to be layered”, intransitive), 重ねる (kasaneru, “to overlap, to layer”, transitive),.
The term originally refers to a bundle of reeds or sedges used as a rain hat. Following the spread of folding umbrellas in the 900s after their introduction from Baekje or China, the sense gradually shifted to also mean "umbrella".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 唐 (kara, “Chinese; foreign”) + 傘 (kasa, “raingear”). First attested in the Utsubo Monogatari of the late 900s.
Folding umbrellas were originally introduced from overseas, likely either Baekje or China, and this term was coined to refer specifically to this style of raingear, as distinct from the traditional Japanese rain hat.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 傘 (MC sanX). Not found in isolation.
The eighty sense is from 仐, the ryakuji or "abbreviated character" form of this kanji, which looks like 八 (“eight”) on top of 十 (“ten”), equating to 八十 (hachijū, “eighty”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/di t͡ɕin/ → /d͡ʑiɕiɴ/
From Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese compound 地震 (MC dijH tsyinH). First cited to a text from 734.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/nawi/ → */nawʲi/ → /naji/ → /nai/
From Old Japanese. First cited to 720 in the Nihon Shoki.
Apparently this term semantically first referred to the ground, and was used most in constructions like ないふる (naifuru, “the ground shakes”). Over time, this shifted via metonymy to refer to the shaking itself.
May be a compound of 土(な) (na, “ground”, possibly an apophonic form of ni, "earth, soil") + 居(ゐ) (i, “being”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of 居(ゐ)る (iru, “to be”, in a location; in modern Japanese, used of animate objects)).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/nawi/ → */nawʲi/ → /naji/ → /naje/ → /nae/
Appears in the Nippo Jisho.
Shift from nai, historical nawi (see above). First cited to the late 1400s.
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 地 (ji, “ground”) + 震い (furui, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of classical Japanese verb 震ふ (furufu, “to tremble; to roar”), related to modern 震える (furueru)). The furui changes to burui as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 山 (yama). First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Reconstructed as deriving in turn from Proto-Japonic *yama (“mountain; forest”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 山 (MC srean).
Sometimes spelled with rendaku (連濁), as -zan.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, itself apparently a borrowing from Old Korean. See Korean 뫼 (moe) for more.
The phonetic man'yōgana spelling 牟礼 for mure appears first in the Kojiki of 720 CE, but instead for the stem of verb 群れる (mureru, “to group together”). The first instance of this spelling for the mountain sense is in the Heian period, in different 日本書紀私記 (Nihon Shoki Shiki) versions, themselves recompilations of the Nihon Shoki. This reading with this sense apparently arises from the traditional 訓読 (kundoku) of a particular section of the Nihon Shoki, where the written word 山 is read as mure with an apparent meaning of mountain or hill.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 川 (kapa), from Proto-Japonic *kapa.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Literary Chinese, possibly early Mandarin 蒲團／蒲团 (pútuán), likely as part of the importation of Zen Buddhism, for which practice these were originally used. First cited in Japanese to a text from the early-mid 1200s with the "meditation cushion" sense.
Originally referred literally to a 蒲 (pú, “bulrush, cattail”) 團／团 (tuán, “ball”), from the way these were round cushions made from woven bulrush leaves.
After the term was borrowed, the usage and construction of these cushions changed and the connection with bulrushes was weakened, leading to the simpler character 布 (fu, “cloth”) being used as a replacement for 蒲 (fu, “bulrush, cattail”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 床(とこ) (toko, “raised floor”) + 屋(や) (-ya, “shop”), due to how barbershops were historically often 床店(とこみせ) (tokomise, “stall with a raised floor used as a store”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ki₂⟩ → */kɨ/ → /ki/
From Old Japanese 木 (ki₂), from Proto-Japonic *kəi. Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *ke. For the vowel alternation, see Wiktionary:About Proto-Japonic § Standalone forms and combining forms.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ko₂⟩ → */kə/ → /ko/
From Old Japanese 木 (ko₂).
Likely the original form of ki above. Obsolete in modern Japanese, never found in isolation; only found in compounds and certain idioms.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 木 (MC muwk). Compare modern Cantonese 木 (muk⁶).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 木 (MC muwk). Compare literary Min Nan 木 (bo̍k).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mura.
Either formed from the nominalization of 群れる (mureru, “to gather”), or from Old Korean. In Old Korean toponyms, this appears with the phonetic spelling 牟羅 (*mura). Compare Korean 무리 (muri, “group, crowd”), also possibly cognate with 群れる (mureru, “to gather”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 村 (MC tshwon).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First mentioned in the Man'yōshū, completed in 759 CE.
Derives from the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 生やす (hayasu, “to grow”). The root verb is in the transitive form, suggesting that the original sense of hayashi may have indicated a deliberately planted or managed grove.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/rimʉ/ → /riɴ/
From Middle Chinese 林 (MC lim).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in the mid-Muromachi period.
Derivation unclear, likely theories include:
* May be cognate with 露 (tsuyu, “dew, dewdrop”), from the way the rainy season causes everything to be covered in drops that may look like dew. However, the pitch accent differs, as 露 (tsuyu) has either an 頭高型 (atamadaka-gata) or 尾高型 (odaka-gata) pattern, while 梅雨 (tsuyu) has a 平板型 (heiban-gata) pattern.
* Alternatively, may be cognate with classical verb 熟ゆ (tsuyu, modern 熟える (tsueru), “to become ripe”), as plums ripen during the rainy season. In light of the pitch accent and semantics, this derivation appears more likely.
The spelling is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 梅雨.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese compound 梅雨 (MC mwoj hjuX), in poetic reference to the season when plums grow or ripen.
Alternatively, the 黴雨 spelling may have been the original spelling. This is homophonous in Middle Chinese, and literally means “mold + rain”, in reference to how moldy things get during this season of constant humidity.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE).
Probably cognate with 盛り (mori, “heap, pile”), the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 盛る (moru, “to heap up, to build up into a significant amount”), from the way a forest can look like a heap or mound from a distance.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pasi/ → /ɸasi/ → /hasi/
From Old Japanese, originally indicating either the area between two things, or a connection between two things.
Cognate with 階 (hashi, “stairs from a garden up to the house”), both cognate with root hasa indicating the narrow area between two things, as in 狭間 (classical hasama, modern hazama, “narrow gap between two things”) or 挟む (hasamu, “to put between two things that are close together, to squeeze between two things”). Cognate also with root hoso indicating the narrowness of a thing itself, as in 細い (hosoi, “narrow, slender”), 細める (hosomeru, “to narrow something, to make something narrow”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, with the original meaning of “plot of land”. Vovin argues it is likely borrowed from an ancestor to Middle Korean 맡 (math, “field”) , but all Japanese etymological theories base the etymology on the meaning of “town; section of a castle town”, typically using 道(ち) (chi), 道(みち) (michi, “road”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 町 (MC thengX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 皮肉 (MC bje nyuwk), literally “skin and meat”.
Originally a Buddhist term from the Zen expression 皮肉骨髄 (“skin, flesh, bones, and marrow”) used to evaluate disciples’ understanding, where “bones and marrow” represent the core truth, and “skin and meat” symbolize the superficial understanding.
As a result, it came to refer to shallow criticism (pointing out faults without addressing the essence) and irony in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨aki₁⟩ → */akʲi/ → /aki/
From Old Japanese.
Likely cognate with 明き (aki, “bright”), 赤 (aka, “red”), 飽きる (akiru, “to become full up”, possibly in reference to the harvest), 空く (aku, “to become empty”), 開く (aku, “to open up”). However, the exact relationship of these terms remains unclear.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined by Maeno Ryōtaku in 1777.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ko₂me₂⟩ → */kəməj/ → /kome/
From Old Japanese. First appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 渠(こ)梅(め). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *kəmay.
Many theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation:
* Perhaps from 籠(こ)め (kome), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 籠(こ)める (komeru, “to do with one's heart”)., from the way rice is farmed. The accent of kome in the Heian period is , while kome- in the Heian period is .
* Possibly cognate with Proto-Vietic *kəːm (“cooked rice”), modern cơm.
* Possibly cognate with Proto-Austronesian *Semay and Old Chinese 糜 (OC *mral). However, this is extremely speculative; none of the known derivations from Proto-Austronesian *Semay develop initial /k/, nor is this shift explainable by any known mechanism within Japonic.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨yo₂nai⟩ → */jənai/ → */jəne/ → /jone/
First attested in the Wamyō Ruijushō (938 CE).
From Proto-Japonic *yənəi; possibly related to 稲 (ine, “rice plant”).
The colloquial sense is derived from the components of the 米 kanji: 八 (hachi, “eight”) + 十 (jū, “ten”) + 八 (hachi, “eight”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Probably a shortened reduplication of kome (see above).
First cited to a work from 1275.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 米 (MC mejX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pa/ → /ɸa/ → /ha/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pa.
Probably cognate with Old Japanese verb 生(は)ゆ (hayu, “to sprout, to grow”) → modern 生(は)える (haeru), and with 羽(は) (ha, “feather; wing”).
Suggested in some sources as possibly cognate with 歯(は) (ha, “tooth”), from the way that both sprout and then later fall, and with 刃(は) (ha, “blade”) from similarities in shape (cf. English blade). However, the pitch accent patterns are different; 葉 and 羽 are both unaccented, while 歯 and 刃 are both accented. This may reflect two disparate *pa roots in the ancient language.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE with the phonetic spelling 波.
Cognate with Okinawan 葉 (fā).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/epu/ → /efu/ → /eu/ → /joː/
From Middle Chinese 葉 (MC yep, “leaf”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨nizi⟩ → /niʑi/
From Old Japanese 虹 (nizi), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *nonsi. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Also attested as man’yōgana form 爾自 in the 金光明最勝王経音義 (Konkōmyō Saishōō-kyō Ongi) of 1079. May be a shift from earlier ぬじ (nuji) or のじ (noji) readings.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 虹 (MC huwng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 都合 (MC tu kòp, “to sum up; altogether”). First attested in Japan in the 正倉院文書 (Shōsōin Monjo) of 734 CE in the literal sense of “totaling” or “summing up.”
Over time, the meaning shifted from the “total sum of things” to the “general state of affairs” (circumstances) in the Middle Japanese period, eventually leading to the modern sense of “convenience.”

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 明(あ)ける (akeru, “to dawn”) and 空(あ)ける (akeru, “to empty”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ame₂⟩ → */aməɨ/ → /ame/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *amay.
Cognate with 天 (ame, unbound apophonic of ama, “sky”), as in the location of clouds where water precipitates from.
Distinct from 飴 (⟨ame₁⟩ → ame, “candy”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *amay.
A bound apophonic form only appearing in compounds. Compare the formation of 目(ま) (ma, bound form in compounds) and 目(め) (me, standalone form), 手(た) (ta) and 手(て) (te), 風(かざ) (kaza) and 風(かぜ) (kaze), or 酒(さか) (saka) and 酒(さけ) (sake).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 雨 (MC hjuX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kumo₁⟩ → */kumʷo/ → /kumo/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kumo.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 雲 (MC hjun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of 神(かみ) (kami, “god, spirit”) + 鳴(な)り (nari, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 鳴(な)る (naru, “to cry out, to call”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kaminari/ → /kamʉnari/ → /kanːari/
Shift in pronunciation from kaminari above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ika tu ti⟩ → ⟨ikaduti⟩ → /ikad͡zut͡ɕi/ → /ikazut͡ɕi/
From Old Japanese.
Originally a compound of 厳(いか) (ika, “sternness, terribleness, imposingness”) + つ (tsu, Old Japanese possessive particle) + 霊(ち) (chi, “spirit, force, essence”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 鳴(な)る (naru, “to cry out, to call”) + 神(かみ) (kami, “god, spirit”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 雷 (MC lwoj).
Compare modern Mandarin 雷 (léi) and Cantonese 雷 (leoi⁴).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 電(でん) (den, “electric”) + 車(しゃ) (sha, “vehicle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨simo₁⟩ → /simo/ → /ɕimo/
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Harima Fudoki of 715 CE, in turn from Proto-Japonic *simo.
Thought to be cognate with or derived from 下(しも) (⟨simo₁⟩ → shimo, “bottom, lower part”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 霧(き)る (kiru, “to become foggy”).
First attested in 712 CE in the Kojiki, in the sense "breath expelled from a person".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨tuyu⟩ → /t͡suju/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨arapa⟩ → /araɸa/ → /arawa/
From Old Japanese.
Cognate with prefix 粗 (ara-, “crude, raw”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 露 (MC luH).
; “Russia”
Short-form of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)) spelling 露西亜.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kansai.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kansai.
A bound apophonic form only appearing in compounds. Compare the formation of 目(ま) (ma, bound form in compounds) and 目(め) (me, standalone form), 手(た) (ta) and 手(て) (te), 雨(あま) (ama) and 雨(あめ) (ame), or 酒(さか) (saka) and 酒(さけ) (sake).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from Old Japanese 風 (ti), modern chi above, found in some compounds.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. May be related to chi above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/puː/ → /fuː/
From Middle Chinese 風 (MC pjuwng).
In Old Japanese, this kanji was used to transcribe the 借音 (shakuon) kana of ⟨pu⟩ and ⟨bu⟩ in the Nihon Shoki (720 CE).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ame₁⟩ → */amʲe/ → /ame/
From Old Japanese.
Distinct from 雨 (⟨ame₂⟩ → ame, “rain”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Simplified from 驛 (睪 → 尺).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 驛 (yek, “relay station (a place for changing horses in pre-modern times)”). First attested in Japanese in 718.
